question:
The figure below shows a tiling of \(1 \times 1\) unit squares. Each row of unit squares is shifted horizontally by half a unit relative to the row above it. A shaded square is drawn on top of the tiling. Each vertex of the shaded square is a vertex of one of the unit squares. In square units, what is the area of the shaded square?

[Figure 1](figures/2026_AMC_8_Q13_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Enclose the shaded square in a larger square whose sides are horizontal and vertical. The unshaded corners will have areas that are easy to calculate.

[Figure 1](figures/2026_AMC_8_Q13_question_fig1.svg)

For the shaded side joining the leftmost and topmost vertices, count across the row between them: the horizontal distance is \(3\) unit widths, and the vertical distance is \(1\) unit. From the topmost vertex to the rightmost vertex, the horizontal distance is \(1\) unit and the vertical distance is \(3\) units.

Thus the enclosing square has width and height \(3+1=4\). Between it and the shaded square are four right triangles, each with perpendicular legs \(1\) and \(3\). These triangles have nonoverlapping interiors and fill all the unshaded space inside the enclosing square.

Each triangle has area \(\frac{1\cdot3}{2}\), so the shaded area is
\[
4\cdot4-4\left(\frac{1\cdot3}{2}\right)
=16-6=10.
\]
The area is \(10\) square units, choice A.
